cases.name: ast: keys and a count
cases.notes: `group by` is a `groupBy` node of keys (each `key` shaped like a select item); an aggregate call is an `aggregate` node, not a `call`.
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows) from people group by city

cases.name: ast: an expression key with its alias, having, order by an aggregate
cases.query: select d, n: count($rows) from people group by d: age / 10 having count($rows) > 1 order by count($rows) desc

cases.name: ast: `distinct` moved to the collection — a reduction is a plain call
cases.query: select names: collect($rows { select distinct name values }), n: count($rows { select distinct pay values }) from people group by city
cases.notes: GRAMMAR §4: there is no `aggregate` node and no `distinct` call modifier. `collect($rows { select distinct name values })` is a `call` whose one argument is an `op` over `$rows` carrying the `select distinct`, which is the `distinct` the language already had.

cases.name: ast: the default projection is the keys plus count
cases.notes: A grouped body without a `select` projects every key by its name and `count: count()`; the parser synthesizes the items (with empty spans), so the tree shows them.
cases.query: from people group by city

cases.name: ast: a grouped nested block, and `$rows count` as a value
cases.notes: §24: the nested block carries its own `groupBy`; `$rows count { … }` is a value-position directive over the `$rows` intrinsic, a receiver like any other.
cases.query: select name, g: jobs collect { group by employer }, n: $rows count { where active } from staff

cases.name: ast spans: group by and a reduction
cases.notes: A reduction spans as the `call` it is — the name through the closing parenthesis (AST.md §4).
cases.query: select k, n: count($rows) from p group by k

cases.name: default projection: the keys plus count, one row per group in first-appearance order
cases.notes: Absent and null keys group together; the key record holds the first row's value (Dan has no city, so the group's `city` is absent and dropped).
cases.query: from people group by city

cases.name: any / all over a per-row predicate, through $rows
cases.notes: §24: `any`/`all` are reductions like the rest — they take a collection and test truthiness of its elements (absent is false, so they do not skip it). A PREDICATE per row is `$rows { p values }`; through 0.28 the aggregate read its argument per row itself.
cases.query: select city, adults: all($rows { age >= 18 values }), senior: any($rows { age > 50 values }) from people group by city

cases.name: $rows is the group's rows as a value
cases.query: select city, $rows from people where city == "NYC" group by city
cases.notes: §24: `$rows` projected bare yields the group's rows themselves, in input order — the raw rows, keyed by the intrinsic's own name.

cases.name: rows as a receiver: collect
cases.query: select city, names: $rows collect { select name } from people group by city

cases.name: rows as a receiver: collect with values and order by (the escape hatch that keeps absent)
cases.query: select city, names: $rows collect { name values order by name }, pays: $rows collect { pay values } from people group by city

cases.name: rows as a receiver: count { … } as a value
cases.query: select city, n: $rows count { where active } from people group by city

cases.name: rows as a receiver: first
cases.query: select city, youngest: $rows first { name values order by age } from people group by city

cases.name: rows as a receiver: single
cases.query: select city, only: $rows single { name values } from people where city == "SF" group by city

cases.name: rows as a receiver: single over several rows is the single error
cases.query: select city, only: $rows single { name values } from people group by city

cases.name: rows as a receiver in having: exists
cases.query: select city from people group by city having $rows exists { where !active }

cases.name: inside a rows block ^ reads the group's keys
cases.query: select city, n: $rows count { where city == ^city } from people group by city

cases.name: rows inside an aggregate's argument is a row property
cases.query: select t, s: sum(rows) from teams group by t

cases.name: rows outside a grouped body is an ordinary property
cases.query: select rows from teams

cases.name: group and having are field names outside their position
cases.query: select group, having from things where group == "x"

cases.name: $it at the group scope is the key record and $key its structural identity
cases.query: select city, it: $it, k: $key from people group by city

cases.query: select label: `${city}: ${count($rows)}` from people where has(city) group by city

cases.name: having filters the groups
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows) from people group by city having count($rows) > 1

cases.name: having may name a select alias
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows) from people group by city having n > 1

cases.name: having may read a key
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows) from people group by city having has(city)

cases.name: having without group by
cases.query: from people having count($rows) > 1

cases.name: order by an aggregate, then a key; absent keys sort last
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows) from people group by city order by count($rows) desc, city

cases.name: order by a key
cases.query: select city values from people group by city order by city

cases.name: order by reads a select alias at the group scope (0.27)
cases.notes: Through 0.26 `order by` was not rewritten against the select, so `n` was an unknown name there; since 0.27 every row-reading clause sees the body's aliases — `order by n` is `order by count()`.
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows) from people group by city order by n desc, city

cases.name: limit and offset bound the groups
cases.query: select city values from people group by city limit 1 offset 1

cases.name: a non-key bare name reads its PER-ROW LIST (0.29)
cases.notes: §24: the headline of 0.29. A bare name at the group scope is the host's — a key reads the key, any other property reads the list of its value across the group's rows, one element per row. Through 0.28 this was a parse error and a grouped body could not read a row field at all.
cases.query: select name from people group by city

cases.name: a dotted read of a non-key is absent — the head is the per-row LIST
cases.notes: §24 + §1: `meta` at the group scope is the per-row LIST of each row's `meta`, and navigating `.city` from a list is absent (§1 "navigating from absent yields absent" applies to a non-object alike), so the property is dropped. To reach each row's `meta.city` descend into the rows: `$rows { meta.city values }`.
cases.query: select meta.city from people group by name

cases.name: a key may be navigated and operated on at the group scope
cases.query: select up: city.upper(), big: count($rows) > 1 from people group by city

cases.name: select distinct with group by is redundant
cases.query: select distinct city from people group by city

cases.name: a directive's distinct with group by is redundant too
cases.query: people collect distinct { group by city }

cases.name: group by after order by is the clause-order error
cases.query: from people order by city group by city

includes: select, from, where, frontier, follow, flatten, group by, having, order by, limit, offset

cases.name: follow after group by is the clause-order error
cases.query: from tree group by id follow kids

cases.name: group by with nothing after it
cases.query: from people group by

cases.name: duplicate group key
cases.query: from people group by city, city

cases.name: a key named count needs an explicit select
cases.query: from people group by count: city

includes: a group key named `count` needs an explicit `select`

cases.name: a key named count with an explicit select is fine
cases.query: select count, n: count($rows) from people group by count: city

cases.name: an unknown free call is an eval error — the reduction names are reserved
cases.notes: GRAMMAR §1: `count sum min max avg collect first last any all` are the language's, so a host cannot serve a function under one of them; every OTHER free call is the host's and an unserved one is the ordinary unknown-function eval error. Through 0.28 this was a parse error naming the aggregate list.
cases.query: select city, m: median(age) from people group by city

cases.name: $rows is TOTAL: a reduction in an ungrouped body is per-row
cases.notes: §24: with no `group by`, `$rows` is `[$it]` — a row is a group of one — so `count($rows)` is 1 on every row and the body still yields one row per row. Through 0.28 a reduction outside a grouped body was a parse error. This is what closes the 0.28 trap where `sum($rows { … })` parsed, found `$rows` unknown at row scope and silently reduced to 0.
cases.query: select n: count($rows) from people

cases.name: order by a reduction in an ungrouped body: per-row, so the order is unchanged
cases.notes: §24: `$rows` is `[$it]` pre-group, so `count($rows)` is 1 on every row and the sort is stable in source order. Legal since 0.29; a parse error through 0.28.
cases.query: from people order by count($rows)

cases.name: a reduction written directly in `where` is legal and PER-ROW
cases.notes: §24 "Staging": `$rows` is legal in every clause — `[$it]` before `group by`. So `count($rows) > 1` is `1 > 1` per row, false, and the result is empty. Only the ALIAS indirection is refused (the next case). Through 0.28 any aggregate in `where` was a parse error.
cases.query: from people where count($rows) > 1 group by city

cases.name: staging: a `where` may not read a select alias that reads $rows
cases.notes: §24 "Staging" — the one thing the rule refuses, and the ALIAS is what is judged, never the function. `n` is written for the group scope; §14 would inline it into `where`, which runs before `group by`, where `$rows` is `[$it]` — so it would answer 1 for every row. Silently-one is worse than a refusal. The same text written directly in `where` is accepted (the previous case).
cases.query: select n: count($rows) from people where n > 1 group by city

cases.name: a group key may read $rows — pre-group it is [$it]
cases.notes: §24 "Staging": a key is evaluated per row, before the grouping, so `$rows` there is `[$it]` and `count($rows)` is 1 on every row — one group, keyed 1. Useless but well-defined, and NOT the staging error, which is about the alias indirection alone. A parse error through 0.28.
cases.query: from people group by k: count($rows)

cases.name: reductions NEST — nothing about them is special any more
cases.notes: GRAMMAR §4: `sum(count($rows))` reduces the number `count($rows)` returns — `toList` makes a lone value one element, so the sum is that number. Through 0.28 this was the parse error `an aggregate cannot nest`, which existed only because an aggregate's argument was read per row by the function.
cases.query: select city, x: sum(count($rows)) from people group by city

cases.name: a reduction needs its collection
cases.notes: GRAMMAR §4: arity is one argument, the collection — there is no zero-argument form since `count()` stopped meaning "the group's rows". The message names both spellings.
cases.query: select city, s: sum() from people group by city

cases.name: an aggregate takes one argument
cases.query: select city, s: sum(age, 1) from people group by city

cases.name: the `distinct` CALL modifier is retired — it belongs to the collection
cases.notes: GRAMMAR §4: `distinct` is no longer a call modifier, so `any(distinct active)` does not parse; dedupe with the collection's own `select distinct` — `count($rows { select distinct active values })`. Through 0.28 `distinct` stood after the opening parenthesis and was rejected on `any`/`all` with a bespoke message.
cases.query: select city, a: any(distinct active) from people group by city

cases.name: a grouped nested block in a projection
cases.query: select name, byEmp: jobs collect { employer, total: sum(pay) group by employer } from staff

cases.name: a nested count over groups counts the groups
cases.query: select name, n: jobs count { group by employer } from staff

cases.name: a where-position test over groups
cases.query: name from staff where jobs exists { group by employer having count($rows) > 1 }

cases.name: a where-first block body may group
cases.query: name, n: jobs count { pay > 1 group by employer } from staff

cases.name: the top-level count directive counts the groups
cases.query: people count { group by city }

cases.name: the top-level first directive is the first group
cases.query: people first { group by city }

cases.name: exists over groups honors having
cases.query: people exists { group by city having count($rows) > 2 }

cases.name: a single receiver grouped is one record
cases.query: person { group by city }

cases.name: an empty source has no groups
cases.query: select city, n: count($rows), s: sum(pay) from people group by city

cases.name: group by over a walk groups the occurrences
cases.query: select d, n: count($rows), ids: collect(id) from tree follow kids group by d: $depth

cases.name: count { … } is a value outside grouping too
cases.query: select name, n: jobs count { where pay > 1 }, big: jobs count { } > 2 from staff

cases.name: exists and none stay where-position tests
cases.query: select name, e: jobs exists { } from staff

cases.name: references: keys in clause groupBy; a reduction's argument is a GROUP read
cases.notes: AST.md §5b, 0.29: a reduction's argument is an ordinary expression of the scope it stands in, so `sum(pay)` references `pay` at the GROUP scope — where it reads the per-row list — not on the rows. Through 0.28 an `aggregate` node on the path demoted it to a row read. `$rows` is the language's value and is not a reference.
cases.query: select city, n: sum(pay), names: $rows collect { select name where age > ^lo } from people where active group by city, lo: age having count($rows) > 1 order by city

steps.expr: group by city: city, lo: age
group by city: city, lo: age
group by city: city, lo: age

cases.name: references: a having alias and an order-by key are not references
cases.query: select n: count($rows { select distinct name values }) from people group by city having n > 1 order by count($rows), city
cases.notes: §14: `having n > 1` reads a select alias, not a row field, so it is no reference; the `order by` key likewise. Inside `$rows { select distinct name values }` the `name` is a row read, one scope deeper, because the BLOCK re-enters the rows — not because the reduction does.

cases.name: references: a key name inside a reduction's argument is a GROUP read
cases.notes: 0.29 inverts this case. `collect(city)` references `city` at the group scope (the key), and `size($rows)` reads the intrinsic, which is no reference. Through 0.28 the aggregate's argument was read per row, so `city` there was a ROW read of the same name — the one place the old rule was genuinely confusing.
cases.query: select k: city, cs: collect(city), n: size($rows) from people group by city

cases.name: references: a grouped nested block
cases.query: select name, g: jobs collect { employer, t: sum(pay) group by employer } from staff
cases.notes: A nested block is its own scope: its `groupBy` key and its reduction's argument are references of THAT body's group scope, one depth deeper.
